title: Fiber Reconciler: Fiber Node Linked List, Work Loop, and Time Slicing
prerequisites: Browser Event Loop and call stack

progressiveExplaining.eli5: In the old days, React was like a chef who had to finish baking 100 cookies in one continuous marathon without taking a single breath—if the doorbell rang, nobody could answer it. React Fiber turned the recipe into a step-by-step checklist. The chef bakes one cookie, quickly checks if the doorbell rang (user click), and if not, bakes the next cookie. If someone rings, the chef pauses immediately to answer.
progressiveExplaining.junior: The Fiber Reconciler is React's core engine for updating the UI. Instead of recursive function calls (the old Stack reconciler), Fiber represents every component instance and DOM element as a mutable node in a singly-linked list tree (`child`, `sibling`, `return`). This enables **Time Slicing**: React splits rendering work into 5ms chunks, yielding control back to the browser between chunks to keep the page responsive to clicks and typing.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Fiber splits rendering into two distinct phases: (1) the **Render Phase** (asynchronous, interruptible, can be paused, aborted, or restarted), and (2) the **Commit Phase** (synchronous, uninterruptible DOM mutation). During the Render Phase, the work loop executes `performUnitOfWork(fiber)` walking the `workInProgress` tree. Fiber uses **Double Buffering**: React maintains two trees—the `current` tree (currently on screen) and the `workInProgress` tree (built in memory)—swapping the root pointer atomically in the commit phase.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: A `FiberNode` contains structural pointers (`child`, `sibling`, `return`), state hooks (`memoizedState`), props (`memoizedProps`, `pendingProps`), and work tags (`flags`, `subtreeFlags`, `lanes`). The work loop runs `while (workInProgress !== null && !shouldYield()) { workInProgress = performUnitOfWork(workInProgress); }`. `shouldYield()` uses a 5ms frame deadline via `MessageChannel` / `performance.now()`. In `beginWork()`, React computes diffs and updates state; in `completeWork()`, it bubbles up `subtreeFlags` and builds the host DOM instances.

interviewGotchas.question: Why is the Render Phase interruptible, but the Commit Phase must be synchronous and uninterruptible?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your understanding of UI consistency and visual tearing.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The Render Phase only creates and mutates in-memory JavaScript objects (the `workInProgress` Fiber tree); pausing or discarding it has zero visible effect on the user. The Commit Phase, however, applies physical DOM mutations (`appendChild`, `removeChild`, attribute updates). If the Commit Phase were paused halfway through, the user would see a partially updated, broken UI (visual tearing). Therefore, the Commit Phase must execute synchronously from start to finish.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Never say that React modifies the real DOM during `beginWork` or `completeWork`. Real DOM mutations happen strictly in the Commit Phase.

interviewGotchas.question: What is 'Double Buffering' in React Fiber?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Tests knowledge of graphics rendering concepts applied to the Fiber architecture.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Similar to graphics engines swapping video frame buffers, React maintains two complete Fiber trees: the `current` tree (representing the DOM currently visible on screen) and the `workInProgress` tree (a draft tree being constructed during the render phase). Each fiber node has an `.alternate` pointer to its twin in the other tree. When rendering completes, React swaps a single pointer (`root.current = workInProgress`), making the draft tree the new current tree in an `O(1)` step.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: React does not destroy and re-allocate the `current` tree from scratch; it recycles existing fiber nodes via the `alternate` pointer to reduce garbage collection pressure.
